name: RoboDojo
summary: RoboDojo argues that existing benchmarks are either simulation-only or real-only and mostly short-horizon and skill-narrow, so they cannot say much about a generalist policy. It bundles 42 simulation tasks scored along five explicit dimensions — generalization, memory, precision, long-horizon execution and open-vocabulary instruction following — with 18 real-world tasks, behind an integration layer that runs a policy in both with minimal modification. The distinguishing piece is RoboDojo-RealEval: standardized hardware offered through cloud access with fixed protocols, so a real-robot number can be reproduced by someone who does not own the robot. Led by HKU's MMLab with roughly twenty institutions including Berkeley and Tsinghua, it launched with a public leaderboard and 30 integrated policies.
innovation: Real-robot evaluation as a hosted service on standardized hardware, removing the lab-specific setup that makes real numbers incomparable.
Scores decomposed into five capability axes rather than one success rate, so memory and precision failures are visible separately.
matters: Complements RoboArena's crowd-sourced ranking with a reproducible fixed-protocol counterpart — between them, real-robot claims finally have somewhere to be checked.
limits: Cloud real-robot access is a queue and a fixed hardware choice, which bounds throughput and generality.
New enough that leaderboard coverage is uneven across the policies that matter.
lineage: LIBERO and SimplerEnv's simulated suites joined to RoboArena's insistence on real-robot evidence.
